we were receiving the same evasive, the same irresponsible answers.
I think the Canadian people have had enough of those ways of administering the country, of that trend given to Canadian politics and the economy. We want action and frankness not only in words but in action, we want the government and public men to grapple directly with problems and to take efficient measures so as to arrive at a settlement before the mountain brings forth all its grievances and all its uneasiness.
The railway companies also, Mr. Speaker, have not assumed all their responsibilities, because they did not offer definite wages and labour conditions, leaving to the central government the burden of paying the bill, of showing imagination and leadership. That is why in that conflict, at the table of negotiations, the ghost presence of the central government could be felt.
In the face of that situation, considering the discussion on the strike in general, on the strike in the public services, the principles connected with the railway strike which must be settled rapidly, as a result of those considerations, it is in order to suggest a few reforms in the part we must play as legislators. That is our main function here in this parliament. We are not here to multiply political partisanships. We are not here to bring up like popcorn being made the positions taken by a political party when in the opposition if it takes the opposite position when in power. We are here to legislate and, in the field of labour, it is urgent, Mr. Speaker, to bring forth reforms.
I want to submit to the attention of this house a few reforms and I would greatly appreciate it if the government would consider them with all the other recommendations and judicious suggestions submitted by other members during the present debate.
First, it is urgent to set up an adequate labour legislation. Second, we need labour-management courts able to decide fairly with regard to professional conflicts.
Third, until we get that appropriate legislation and those labour-management courts, we must leave management and labour free to exercise their defence rights, namely the right to strike or appeal.
In addition, in the process of evolution, civil conflicts are settled today by the courts, whereas at the beginning of the world individuals took justice into their own hands. In the era of the cavemen, if another man stole his neighbour's cattle, there were no

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters courts. The offended party took justice into his own hands: the right to own things. And that right goes with the right to defend oneself and that right must be exercised until the day when appropriate legislation and courts exist. Then the exercise of that right of defence in civil and criminal matters is given to the duly constituted courts which we have today.
That is why I say that the right to strike or lockout is temporary until we have adequate legislation and courts. It is false to think that the right to strike in itself or the lockout is absolute, eternal and unlimited. The responsibility falls on the state and on us legislators to create legislation and labour-management courts.
It is also incumbent on the state to promote the creation of organizations which will create a balance in the economic and social fields between the state, management and labour.
Here is my fourth reform or suggestion. I propose the setting up of a wisemen court which a national management confederation and a general labour confederation should put to work. I am thinking in particular of an organization similar to the labour market commission in Sweden.
That organization which we could set up should take into account our Canadian and constitutional characteristics. Mr. Speaker, this afternoon a few allusions were made to Sweden. I am not talking at all about the political system, socialist or otherwise, of Sweden.
But when we look squarely at the problems, we can take good ideas in every country and every political creed. We can take an idea or a structure which gave excellent results for the common good of a country without for all that accepting the philosophy or political theories of the Swedish government, since that one was mentioned this afternoon, if it is really a socialist government.
There is a wisemen court there wh;ch is called the labour market commission. It was created in 1937 between a national management confederation and a national labour confederation.
And I reach this point to say, as I pointed out a while ago, that in this dispute the unions also have some responsibilities, as well as the employers, the management, in Canada. At this time, in the dispute we are facing eight railway companies; on the other hand, we have 16 or 18 unions formed into

The management, the employers, got together into a national confederation, and the unions forgot their differences, their local or regional peculiarities and grouped together to consider the wider problems in a national trade unions confederation.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
And the two organizations of both confederations met and established a basic agreement which has enabled them, since 1937, to set the labour disputes. And thus, since 1937, Sweden has had no strikes. Whether the government of that country be communist, socialist, or capitalist, we have there a wonderful idea which has been applied and I would appreciate it very much if the government and, mainly the management parties and the unions, instead of fighting so much, instead of acting in such an individualistic way would seek to pool their interests. We would have both levels of interest on a national level, with capital and labour meeting together and setting out standards in an agreement as was done in Sweden.
We could also consider renovating here, for instance, in Canada, if it took too long for the good faith of the Canadian labour and management to achieve this organization, the National Labour Relations Board and have it play a similar role.
It is absolutely necessary that there should be established, between management and labour in Canada, permanent structures which would enable them to achieve their goal, to promote better social and economic balance, and to make a contribution to the achievement of the commonweal. And in this fourth reform that I suggest, Mr. Speaker, I would see very favourably the government, in turn, co-operate with the provinces and establish an organization of experts who would analyse eventual disputes, which we can see coming, and who would then keep people informed.
Oh, how Canada lacks objective organizations which would be backed and encouraged by the government and which would comprise university professors, experts in economics, actuaries, experts in industrial relations and in the taxation areas, that is groups of perhaps 12 persons, who would work in co-operation with the provinces as soon as a dispute could be seen in the offing. Those experts would closely consider the question, make a quick assessment of the causes and
[Mr. Allard.)

the unrest and suggest the remedies and then make sure, as an organization, to publicize it throughout the country through television radio and the newspapers.
During conversations I had in a bus-I was going to say in a train, but there are not any for some hours to come-and on the street here, in Ottawa, and elsewhere, I asked several people this point-blank question: What do you think, sir or madam, of the strike- What would you suggest about the railway strike in Canada? Some would have no opinion, others would express very superficial opinions. We do not have the advantage of such an organization.
I know that some members will say that we have the Economic Council of Canada, others are going to say that we have the Quebec economic planning council and, in Ontario, another body along the same line. But the gap is precisely there. We have at the central government an economic planning council working alone and often without correlation as regards the economic planning councils of the provinces. What we need is for an organization to co-operate with the provinces so as to forestall such conflicts. As second point of my remarks, I wanted to deal with the second aspect of this bill, that is, the salary increase.
As mentioned in section 6, the provisional contract provides for 8 per cent a year for two years, that is, 16 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I feel it does not rest with the state to set salary rates in a system of free enterprise. I realize that the government is in a tight corner and has to settle the matter without delay.
That is why, in the face of this nation-wide crisis, I shall vote for the bill. But I am taking the liberty of pointing out that it is not incumbent on the federal government to determine salary rates in a system of free enterprise. Such rates should be decided upon by the immediate employer and the union representatives.
Another point is this. That government and parliament be conscious of the common good and refrain from pursuing electoral goals. I do not know what was the intention of the present federal government in inserting in this bill an increase of salary amounting to 8 per cent; I wonder also on what basis such an 8 per cent increase was arrived at. If I refer to the recent statements made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), I find that this second indication in the bill is

entirely contrary to his warnings about moderation and inflation. If the right hon. Prime Minister and his experts and advisers are really in a position to decide honestly and objectively that the economic and financial situation of the country has reached a point where-the mean salary in the country being, as for the railway workers, $2.20 per hour-in the face of inflation, we should practice moderation and tighten our belts, then a special budget for next fall should be prepared which would increase taxes and add a few more holes in the belt in order that the Canadian taxpayer may feel the pinch since we are living in an inflated economy. If these words were pronounced in all fairness and sincerity, how is it then that a few days later a bill is introduced by the same federal government, which has no jurisdiction on salary standards, announcing an increase of salary in that very bill?
For instance, it would be very amusing, in case the conflict is referred to the arbitration board, if it were decided by the members of the board that the salaries being what they were are corrected to such an extent. This increase appearing in the bill is very amusing. And it would be very amusing, if in the next debate that the right hon. Prime Minister has promised to us on the problems of inflation, and on the increase in the cost of living, it were established after due consideration and an extended debate, that, when some national average is reached, salaries must be frozen. It would be appropriate, however, to permit increase, that is, not to fix a limit for workers earning less than $1.93 per hour in Canada as is the case for the textile workers at Sherbrooke and in important Quebec cities, whose basic rate is $1.18 to $1.59 per hour. These workers are really far from the average rate prevailing in industry in the country, which is $1.93, if I am not mistaken; but with the railways we see already that this average is $2.20. And this is why I say that I will nevertheless vote in favour of the bill, because the situation is desperate; however, I do not approve of this, in other legislation where we could take the time to introduce amendments if we were not facing a national crisis, where the government must determine wages, while this is not its responsibility. This is providing an arbitration procedure before the conclusions are arrived at on the causes of the conflict.
Finally Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks on this third objective of the bill concerning compulsory arbitration.

We have seen in the past, and hon. members mentioned it, labour leaders who, on many occasions, and over the last few days, have voiced grievances against some arbitration boards in general because they have failed, have not studied seriously the problems; it is true-for those who have followed the whole evolution of arbitration boards- often because political friends or greatly incompetent people were appointed, men who knew nothing about industrial techniques, labour-management relations, people who had no idea of economics and finance, taxation and social and economic problems. Such men were appointed there because they were friends and because they had influence, not because of their intelligence and judgment, but rather because of the roundness of their abdomen.
I agree with the hon. members who submitted grievances; it is because those arbitration boards failed in their duty, because their members showed themselves to be incompetent; it does not mean that the institution is not worthy or is basically faulty; far from it and I admit that under the circumstances it is an organization which must be accepted, a special body, and that the government however, if need be, will give us competent, objective and impartial arbitrators.
The arbitrators should be experts and not members of the government or parliament, to repeat what I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, in order always to make a distinction between the executive, the judiciary and the legislative. The arbitrator should give his decision within a limited time.
I noticed in the bill that the whole thing is to go on through mediation until November 15 and that the mediator must report to the Minister of Labour who afterwards must set up an arbitration board. But no time limit is set, unless I am mistaken and do not understand the wording of the bill. We should find in the bill-and I hope that when it is studied in committee, the government will agree to amend that clause so that a time limit is set for the arbitrators to render their decision; of course, there is a deadline with regard to the arbitrator's decision; it must be given within five days to parliament, then parliament must submit it to the session within the five days which will follow a new session but how long are the arbitrators given, if the matter goes

Well, if the government can give me some assurance as to the wording, I cannot find any provision requiring the arbitrators to make a decision in a given time. I would appreciate it very much if a time limit were set for the arbitrators to hold their discussions and submit their report.
Also, the arbitrators should have the legal and financial capacity and secure advisers. Of course, it will perhaps be pointed out to me that this is not authorized by all the acts referred to in this piece of legislation. If it is impossible to proceed directly, indirect means should be sought. Three arbitrators could be appointed but it could happen that only one who would know all about transportation matters; but, not being an actuary, perhaps he would not be able to work out the calculations. He could have the legal and financial capacity of an actuary who could figure out the total cost of granting such a salary increase or of bringing about such and such results within the Canadian economy.
Mr. Ovide Laflamme {Quebec-Montmorency): Mr. Speaker, I only wish to take a few minutes to give the impressions which I was able to gather from the strikers in my riding during an informative meeting I held last night, and also to make a few remarks which I think appropriate concerning the bill now under consideration in this house.
On the one hand, the general impression I got from the strikers I met convinced me beyond doubt that they had no understanding whatsoever of the meaning of the bill under consideration, because they believed that it actually dealt with the salaries of the railway workers.
In my opinion, this bill-and I believe the salary question is a minor one-deals with only two essential and important points. First, the return to work of the railwaymen, because the strike must end at all costs; second, the resumption of negotiations through a process established in the bill. Thus, the government, in settling the problem of the strike which, of course, must end, was anxious to protect, in spite of everyone and even, I submit, against some members of the opposition and especially the N.D.P., the freedom of collective bargaining, even in the field of the public service. On that point, I believe that all Canadian workers presently on strike must understand me.
At the present time the Canadian government has taken care to protect the freedom of collective bargaining, even in the field of public service and railway transportation. Negotiations, of course, provide for a return to work, a sort of sit-down strike, and a salary increase which seems small; however, I believe this is not very important at present since, under this bill, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) will appoint a mediator who will report before two months and a half have elapsed; and consequently, if we are not here, and so that the problem does not have to be brought before parliament, there is a provision for compulsory arbitration because the situation naturally has to come to an end. And even then, the present government, which seeks to respect the freedom of negotiations and, in the public field, the freedom of debate, provides that ten members of parliament may, at the time the arbitrators' decision is handed down, raise the question again in the house to criticize or stress the weaknesses of the decision or, finally, to voice the feelings of workers who could be disatisfied with the conditions imposed in the decision.
But, Mr. Speaker, I really wonder if the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has, in his own way, solved the problem this afternoon. He told the government: Your bill is worth nothing. Send it back and introduce another one. What does it mean on the part of the Leader of the Opposition? What have we got in the way of constructive criticism in such an important situation? I respectfully submit that we have absolutely nothing.
As far as the suggestions made by the N.P.D. are concerned, there is opposition to compulsory arbitration. If there is an area in which I think one can logically conceive compulsory arbitration, it is the area of railway transport, where the rates are determined by a government control board called the Board of Transport Commissioners.
And in the case of compulsory arbitration, the government with logic, has upheld the freedom of speech by allowing ten members to rise and the debate to resume and amendments to be moved by the house. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this does not create any difficulty and I sincerely think, because I have spent part of the evening with strikers, that this bill, being logically and objectively set out, seeks to guarantee in the first place the respect of the right to strike, which is a sacred right of the workers, even in the public sector-as I respectfully submit-and

But, Mr. Speaker, neither do I share the opinion of N.D.P. members, who have just endorsed my remarks, that this is the intent of the bill. Rather, as one who has been a union man for many years, I see something much deeper in the bill before us. I see an attempt made by the government to respect and continue the cherished rights of the unions to negotiate their own settlement, and I see the 4 per cent, and 8 per cent mentioned in the bill, as a very temporary settlement of the problems of the railway workers.
Many in my community work for the railway. Many in the gallery tonight are from my community and I know many of the

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters problems facing men who have spent 10, 15 and 20 years working for the C.P.R. I know of their anxiety and uncertainty. I know of the concern of those working in the dining car section, who see national trains shunted away, who at times see an almost conscious effort to discourage passenger service. One can understand, appreciate, and sympathize with the problems of the workingman who is expected to work for the benefit of the railway, when he is confused, as are many in this house, with policies of the C.P.R. that at times discourage passenger service, rather than encourage it.
I think that the railwayman in Canada has been synonymous with respect and maturity for many years because of the fact that the unions that have been charged with the problems of the workingman have been amongst the more mature and responsible in this country, and I do not share the opinion of those who say there is no room in Canada for international unions.
Rather, I think the stability that has been synonymous with the railway movement in Canada is due in large measure to the maturity and wisdom of those men who have taken time out from their normal work to participate actively in the labour movement, and I for one share their anxiety and confusion at the efforts made in some parts of the country to chip away at the authority and jurisdiction of the international unions.
Much effort has been made in the house to confuse not only the railwaymen but also hon. members as to the intent and purpose of the bill. Speaker after speaker has talked about the 6 per cent and 8 per cent in the same breath as he talked about 30 per cent, but each has failed to mention that the 30 per cent settlement of the longshoremen, and the 30 per cent of the seaway workers, is not 30 per cent immediately but 30 per cent spread over a two year period. Until the unions and management begin to finalize negotiations nobody will know what the eventual and total settlement in wages will be for the workingman.
At the present moment we know that if this bill is accepted and the workers return to work there will be an immediate increase for the men. And I presume they will return, Mr. Speaker, although I imagine it is hard for many of them who have gone through nine tortuous months of negotiation, to do so. However, they are members of mature unions which, in the final analysis, know that the laws of the land must be respected. In this

respect this bill differs from the bill introduced in 1960. That bill simply froze the salaries of the men; it ordered them back to work with no immediate increase. That is the fundamental difference. This bill provides that if the men go back to work they will get some immediate increase. It provides that they go back and negotiate with the railway until November 15 in the light of the published amendments introduced for adoption, of certain parts of the MacPherson report, placing the railways in a better position to be more liberal and more conscious perhaps of the rights and needs of the workers.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) wanted to know where we got the figure of 8 per cent. That is the recommendation of Mr. Justice Munroe to this point, and it is significant that it is a higher settlement than the companies' representative on the board was willing to agree to. I must emphasize, even at the risk of being repetitive, that clause 9 provides for the appointment of a mediator for the distinct purpose of negotiating the increase that I am confident will come as the result of negotiation undertaken in the light of the recommendations that will be introduced, and I mean primarily the recommendations of the MacPherson report.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I must speak on behalf of labour. At first glance it concerns me a little bit that if the MacPherson report is accepted in its entirety, or even partially if it provides for the railways to become more efficient, it could conceivably provide for reduction in the work staff, and thus create more insecurity and anxiety, which leads us on to another historic document with which most hon. members are familiar, the Freedman report.
A month or so before the house recessed I said I thought that in time the Freedman report would become as historic in the annals of labour as the Rand report. I am one member of the house and one supporter of the government who thinks that certain aspects of the Freedman report should be introduced almost simultaneously with any segments of the MacPherson report that are going to provide added revenue for the railways and which-and this is more disquieting for me-could provide for a reduction of the working force.
The time has come for all of us to realize that Canada can only be great and prosperous if all segments of society are respected and their needs looked after. There are too many people in this house and outside it who get

up and castigate labour, who point out wildcat strikes and legitimate strikes, but who forget that for every strike that takes place there are hundreds of agreements signed quietly and fairly.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
The government must do more than look at company profits if it expects labour in all fields, not only the railway labour field, to be responsible in its demands. We are duty bound to look at consumer prices, increased dividends and record profits. We can no longer treat the problems of Canada piecemeal. I would suggest, of course, that by the same criterion the unions themselves are morally bound to settle their differences with the railways by November 15.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of attention to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition who I am sure will be along in a few moments. On three or four occasions he pointed out that the railwaymen were responsible people and that he expected they would go back to work, but that he could not blame them if they did not. This reminds me a little of the funeral oration in Julius Caesar when they kept repeating "Brutus was an honourable man". If I was a cynical type and a real partisan, which I am not, I would say that at times I was left with the impression that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition might have been toying with an invitation to the men not to return. I was pleased at the change in his attitude over night.
I would imagine that some of the responsible members from the west who are concerned with the problems of wheat shipments and members from the maritimes who are concerned with the problems of the maritimes may have suggested to their leader that parliament is here to represent the rights of all Canadians, including the farmers and the workers.
The term compulsory arbitration has been bandied about by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and by the leader of the New Democratic Party. I imag ne that this is supposed to be synonymous with sin; to a railwayman and a labourman it is. In looking back into labour matters which have appeared in Hansard, as far back as 1950, I was intrigued by the legislation introduced in the House of Commons in 1958 to settle the Canadian Pacific Steamships strike in British Columbia. I know that many members of the house who are here tonight were present in 1958. Those who were here will recall that

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters this strike had existed for many many months and had been very disruptive in the field of communications in British Columbia. The minister of labour at the time, the present member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), was plagued by the problem of settling this particular strike; so he introduced a bill, a copy of which I have here, which was nothing more or less than compulsory arbitration. I do not say this to castigate the hon. member, the then minister of labour, because there are circumstances where compulsory arbitration is the only and the last method of settling a problem.
The main feature of that bill, which was introduced by hon. members who now sit in opposition, was that it gave the union members on strike so many hours to get back to work, at the risk of forfeiting their jobs. Since the summer recess was coming up, that same bill included the right to punish the union men by order in council if they disregarded the government's instructions to go back to work. All the way through the debate at the time hon. members, particularly the hon. member for, I think, Skeena (Mr. Howard) or, if not, his deskmate, kept referring to the fact that this was compulsory arbitration. I mention this because for the benefit of labour and the people in the gallery, the hon. member and other members of the Conservative party have tried to create the illusion that they never stooped to compulsory arbitration legislation. Yet that is what they did in 1958.
Mr. Speaker, I then looked through other papers to see what else I could find-what other examples of compulsory arbitration. I came across a rather appealing and interesting document put out by a member of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Skeena, in July of this year. That is untrue and it is misleading. So long as there is a railway system in Canada which treats all parts of Canada fairly, so long will it be necessary to assist those railways, to recompense them for uneconomic services or for services which they will have to provide at less than what the traffic could bear if the regulations were not there.
That is why the Minister of Transport provides in his bill for a freezing of the maritime rates. I am sure the fact that he represents Newfoundland is a mere coincidence, but the fact remains that under this new bill the maritime rates are frozen. Why is that so? It is so because it is impossible to place the burden of the transportation system on the people of the maritimes. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it has been neither wrong nor unwise for the government to have always had something to say with regard to the settlement of wages on the railways, because even the Canadian Pacific Railway is not a private enterprise in the normal sense. No matter how much it is regulated, it must always be regulated for the benefit of the Canadian people.
No one in this house would dare suggest, if he had any sense, that the Crowsnest pass rate be removed because the railways could immediately make tens of millions of dollars per year more if they were able to carry the grain at rates which were even a cent per ton mile instead of the half-cent per ton mile which they are now. When the average freight rate per ton mile is about a cent and three-quarters, the railways carry the grain through the Crowsnest pass at rates established in 1897, and it is right that they should do so because the economy of the country requires it. It is also right that the parliament and the public treasury should give assistance in order that the burden not fall on the farmers alone.
The second error that the Prime Minister made and the government is making is to suggest that there has ever been anything like collective bargaining in railway labour negotiations since the end of the war. It was said with such aplomb as if it were really a

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters matter of fact, although it is sheer nonsense to suggest that there has ever been anything like collective bargaining in railway labour negotiations. The railways just sit down and say "no". I am not guessing; I sat on about six or eight conciliation boards and I remember very distinctly the conciliation board of 1956, chaired by Mr. Eric Taylor and held during one of the most prosperous years in Canada. This was one of the best years for the railways. The railway representatives came before the board and said "We cannot make any offer of money". Mr. Taylor looked at one of the vice presidents of the C.P.R. who was on the witness stand-I think it was the late Mr. Emerson-and said "Mr. Emerson, can you not agree that at least a one-half cent increase might be possible for the C.P.R.?" And Mr. Emerson answered with a straight face, "no". This has been the standard procedure of the railway labour negotiations. The railways sat tight, they made no move either on wages or on fringe benefits, and ever since November 2, 1965 this has been their stand in the present case. As far as I know, and I am sure my information is correct, they have not offered a single cent of increase to the workers up to this very moment.
I ask hon. members and through them I ask the people of Canada: What would anyone here do if he were a member of a union which had served notice ten months ago, and at the end of the ten months not a single cent was offered by the employer? Would he not go on strike? Are the employees of the unions to be condemned for acting in this way in the face of this situation? The fact is that there is no collective bargaining between the railways and the unions. To say "We did not want to interfere with the normal collective bargaining process", as the Prime Minister said yesterday in justification for not having entered earlier into the picture is-and I say this with the greatest respect-sheer self delusion, if not worse. There was no normal collective bargaining process. What he is trying to do today he could have done six months ago. I say to him that six months ago he could undoubtedly have reached a much better settlement from his point of view-not from mine-and much better terms might have been achieved than he is likely to get today, after settlements which have taken place with the dockworkers and the seaway workers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, because such is the case in railway bargaining, people who have had

to do with the settling of railway disputes came to the conclusion in 1950 and 1952-such as Mr. Justice Wilson in 1950 and Mr. Justice Kellock in 1952-that the only way to be fair to the railway workers and the only way to-avoid railway strikes was to set a standard by which the railway employees' earnings may be measured.
It was the railways and not the unions which persuaded those conciliation boards that the proper standard for the earnings of railway non-op workers was a comparison with the earnings of employees of the durable goods industries as set out by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. We did this, and I was party to such a decision by boards on a number of occasions. We did this because we had no illusions that the railway workers really had the right to strike. They have it on paper, but every time they try it and every time they threaten to strike, the boom is lowered because a railway strike is so immediately disastrous to the economy of the nation, if it lasts for some time, that everyone knows that at some point parliament will have to step in and tell the boys to go back to work. Those of us who acted on these conciliation boards recognized this fact. We did not utter pious phrases about the right to strike being a sacred right and then propose legislation that takes it away. It is just sheer rubbish to talk about its being a sacred right if you do not intend to let people exercise it. What good is a right if there is no opportunity to use it? The fact is that it is impossible for the country to permit a long strike of the railway workers, a strike which would really give them victory, because sooner or later parliament would have to step in. We realized that and knew that was the case.
The solution to the problem was to set a standard by which the earnings of the railway workers could be measured. The railways suggested it in 1950 and 1952, and when the standard was applied, not totally, not properly or correctly but in some measure, then the railways started kicking against it and ever since then they have tried to destroy what they themselves originally proposed.
What this bill should have done, in my submission, Mr. Speaker, is to have provided a wage for these employees that measures up to the standard provided by the earnings of durable goods employees, properly adjusted in accordance with the sex distribution, the size of the firm, the greater skills in the railway work force and geographical location

which favours the durable goods industry. It should have provided not a dribbling "four and four" but a 25 per cent increase in rates over a period of two years, which is clearly what the arithmetic of the standard properly applied requires.

I plead with members of this house, let us not fool ourselves; we are setting the rates, and in the long run the government will set the rates if parliament does not. There can be no settlement in a railway dispute about wages unless the government goes in and assists that settlement, and guarantees the railways a way to meet the settlement. So that whether the dispute is settled here or is settled later, it will be either this parliament or this government which will settle it.
I say that it would have been much more sens ble, if we are to pass a law which tells people to go back to work, to have the courage to set the wage increase to which these people are clearly entitled by using a standard which has been established by a number of conciliation boards over a number of years.
There is another problem in connection with the railway force which I feel I must draw to the attention of members of this house. Because of the way in which the increases to the railwaymen have been applied in the past number of years, the gap between the unskilled and the skilled workers on the labour force has continually narrowed. For example, today, in 1966 an electrician, a sheet metal worker, a boilermaker or a carman, people who undertake a five year apprenticeship, have a wage rate per hour of $2.49 and a fraction-less than $2.50 an hour. And these are skilled craftsmen who have had five years apprenticeship. These people are concentrated in the large metropolitan areas of Montreal, Toronto, and now Calgary, to a larger and larger extent as mechanization on the railways has eliminated most of the roundhouses and replaced them with large modern shops. As I say, these men work in large metropolitan areas where their counterparts in industry-I am not talking about people in construction here, but manufacturing industry-receive between 75 cents and $1 more per hour.

I believe it is wrong to state that the bill makes no provision for a determination of the Freedman-type issue. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) made explicit something that is implicit in the bill, namely that there is provision for the arbitrator to deal with this particular aspect of the dispute which we face at the present time. The concern of, especially the trainmen, and others involved in this dispute is understandable with respect to the problem posed in the Freedman report. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I have expressed fully my views on the Freedman report and the kind of guidepost it will establish in the field of industrial relations and labour relations in Canada. This problem cannot be ignored. It is a fact that there is concern among the workers that the institution of technological change during the life of a contract may have consequences in respect of their job security. They have urged that they have an opportunity to negotiate on these changes during the life of an agreement.
Mr. Justice Freedman in his report made the proposal that the ideal solution of this problem is to permit the parties, the unions and the men, to work with proper procedures to cope with the problem. This is Mr. Justice Freedman's principal recommendation. He says that if this fails, legislation can be considered along the following lines; An arbitrator will be appointed to determine whether

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters any change contemplated during the life of the agreement is a material change. Then if he concludes that it is not a material change, management is entitled to institute that change. If he concludes it is a material change, it is to be negotiated at that time or at the end of the agreement. That is Mr. Justice Freedman's proposal.
Hon. gentlemen will have read another report involved in this problem, namely the report of the conciliation board headed by Judge Little. In my view there is an encouraging conclusion with respect to the Freedman report in that particular aspect of the conciliation board report, because there is a large degree of agreement between the union representative and the management representative on the way to cope with the Freedman-type issue. It has not been fully resolved but encouraging steps have been taken, and there is no doubt that further encouraging steps will be taken on a voluntary basis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly intend to do that if the minister will just wait for two or three minutes. I am sure he will understand that any hon. member in this house who has had a long connection with the city of Winnipeg could not but ask the question I did today with considerable feeling.
In the year 1919 we had a strike situation in Winnipeg as a result of which a great many people suffered for many years, and many of them are still suffering. We experienced one of the greatest injustices that ever resulted from a strike situation. I am referring to the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway cancelled all pension rights and privileges that had been earned by its employees up to the time of that strike. It went further and provided that from then on no one over 40 years of age could re-enter the pension plan. The total result, as I say, was that for many years there was a great deal of suffering, and there still is for many older men who have retired from the employ of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Because of this injustice the matter was brought up on the floor of the House of Commons for many years by my predecessor, the late Mr. Woodsworth, and I carried on the effort when I came here to try to get the government to do something to restore those pension rights.
We were not able to have that accomplished, but two things did result. One was a report prepared by an esteemed civil servant, who has been in the gallery both yesterday and today, and I see is still there tonight, Mr. Harris Johnstone, on the whole question. This report was made as a result of an investigation ordered at my request by Mr. Mackenzie King, and the report made it clear that the action of the C.P.R. was wrong. But the government still took the position that there was nothing it could do about the 1919 situation.
However, as a result of our efforts in this matter, as a result of Mr. Johnstone's investigation and report and as a result of the battles on the floor of the House of Commons, we did persuade the Liberal government of that day, under Prime Minister Mackenzie King, to put an amendment into the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation


Act. As a matter of fact, it was one of those rare occasions when a private member's amendment was accepted. Although it was subamended to some extent, the heart of the amendment, as I proposed it, was accepted and it is still incorporated in the act.
May I refer the minister to section 4 (3) (b) of the act. I do not need to read all of it, since some of the words are not relevant, but let me read the significant words:
No employer . . . shall deny to any employee any pension rights or benefits to which he would otherwise be entitled by reason only of his ceasing to work after the 1st day of September, 1948, as the result of a lockout or while taking part in a concerted stoppage of work due to a labour dispute where such lockout or stoppage of work has been enforced by the employer or called by the recognized representative of such employee, as the case may be, after all steps provided or contemplated by law have been taken through negotiation, collective bargaining, conciliation and arbitration to settle such dispute or by reason only of dismissal contrary to this act.
I must say that the wording of that section as it was passed is a lot longer than it was when I first moved the amendment to the statute, but surely the sum and substance of the amendment is very clear. I submit that when it was passed by parliament, parliament knew what it was doing. It did not want the 1919 situation ever to be repeated. It did not want workers to lose their pension rights because they went out on strike, particularly if they went out on a legal strike.
I read in yesterday's Toronto Telegram the terrifying item of news that Mr. Ian Sinclair, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, has threatened that if employees of that company fail to go back to work in the event of the bill which is before the house being passed, they will lose their pension rights. It is this law of the land, which stands against the loss of pension rights to any workers who have gone out on a legal strike, that I should like the minister to convey to Mr. Sinclair.
I appreciated the minister's answer this afternoon when he said that he would send it to Mr. Sinclair; and I appreciated his inquiry tonight as to the precise section to which I was referring. I would point out to him that clause 4(b) of Bill No. C-230 to which the Minister without Portfolio referred this afternoon is really not very helpful because it does not cover what might follow from now on. But the section in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to which I have referred does cover the situation, the men having ceased work because of a strike that was legal in every respect.
Augusi 30, 1966	COMMONS
For any company to threaten that these employees might lose their pension rights is a defiance of the law. It is turning the clock back 50 years in a way, I am sure, this parliament would not stand for. In fact, I believe if by any chance there were any defect in the law, the government would want to correct it, so that no pension rights will be lost because of the present strike.
I would appreciate the minister's underlining his willingness to make it clear that this law must be obeyed.
